vention to extend lifespan in many species, may be attributed to its ability to reduce the occurrence of mitochondrial abnormalities
and attenuate oxidative stress CR reduces the total amount of muscle protein synthesis and the fractional synthesis rate of individual
proteins in rodents, but not the age-related CR was shown to have no effect on the decrease in mitochondrial density (Smith et al.,
2015). These ﬁndings suggest that CR does not increase mitochondrial biosynthesis, but rather maintains mitochondrial function
by protecting existing cellular components (Smith et al., 2015). Furthermore, CRs are resistant to increased apoptotic signaling in
skeletal muscle with aging (Lanza et al., 2012). Notably, CR regulates most of the apoptotic pathways that occur in aging muscle,
including mitochondria, cytokines/receptors, and Ca2þ/ER stress-mediated signals (Lanza et al., 2012).
How does CR regulate sarcopenia, independent of mitochondrial function and apoptosis? CR increases PGC-1a in various
organs such as brain, heart, liver, and visceral adipose tissue. PGC-1a plays a variety of roles, including enhancement of mitochon-
drial biosynthesis, fatty acid oxidation, autophagy activation, neuromuscular junction gene induction, and myokine secretion.
Indeed, Valdez et al. (Dirks and Leeuwenburgh, 2004) showed that lifelong CR in mice signiﬁcantly suppressed abnormalities at
the synapse due to age-related loss protection of motoneurons by PGC-1a. It is known that autophagy in skeletal muscle decreases
